message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"19.1","text":"On the next day Peter came forward rather early in the morning. Seeing Simon waiting for him with many others, he greeted the crowd and began to speak with them. But the moment he began, Simon interrupted and said, “Set aside these long preliminaries of yours and answer me as I question you concerning the matter at hand. For I perceive—as I know from what I have heard from the beginning...—that your sole aim is to use every device to demonstrate that the Creator himself alone is a blameless God, and that, in your resolve, you have so great a longing to insist on this that you even dare to call false certain passages of the writings that plainly accuse him. For this reason, I have resolved today to prove that it is impossible for him, being the creator of everything, to be blameless. I can begin the proof now, provided you answer what I ask you.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὀρθριαίτερον","chosen":"rather early in the morning","rationale":"The comparative adverb indicates an earlier-than-usual or notably early time."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸ προκείμενον πυνθανομένῳ μοι ἀπόκριναι","chosen":"answer me as I question you concerning the matter at hand","rationale":"The rendering preserves both the subject under discussion and Simon’s demand that Peter answer his question."},{"source_quote":"πάσῃ μηχανῇ","chosen":"to use every device","rationale":"μηχανή here denotes a contrivance, method, or strategic means, with Simon’s accusatory force retained."},{"source_quote":"τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτὸν δεῖξαι μόνον ἄμεμπτον εἶναι θεὸν","chosen":"to demonstrate that the Creator himself alone is a blameless God","rationale":"μόνον is taken as singling out the Creator as the one who is a blameless God; it could alternatively be attached more closely to the predicate."},{"source_quote":"καὶ τοσοῦτον προαίρεσιν πόθον ἔχοντα διισχυρίζεσθαι, ὡς καὶ ἐνίας τῶν γραφῶν περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ τολμᾶν ψευδεῖς λέγειν","chosen":"and that, in your resolve, you have so great a longing to insist on this that you even dare to call false certain passages of the writings that plainly accuse him","rationale":"ἔχοντα is taken as resuming σε and therefore referring to Peter, while διισχυρίζεσθαι completes πόθον: Peter longs to insist on his claim. προαίρεσιν is understood as an accusative of respect, ‘in respect of resolve.’ This keeps Peter as the subject of the linked longing, insistence, and daring."},{"source_quote":"περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ","chosen":"passages of the writings that plainly accuse him","rationale":"The personal genitive αὐτοῦ and Simon’s polemical context support the hostile sense ‘speak against’ or ‘accuse,’ though a more neutral rendering such as ‘give an account concerning him’ is lexically possible."},{"source_quote":"ἐάν γε","chosen":"provided","rationale":"The particle γε strengthens the stated condition for beginning the proof."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς ἐπακηκοὼς... ἐπίσταμαι","issue":"The selected edition prints exactly three dots between ἐπακηκοὼς and ἐπίσταμαι, apparently marking unavailable wording or a printed break in the construction. The translation retains exactly three dots and supplies no restoration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"καὶ τοσοῦτον προαίρεσιν πόθον ἔχοντα διισχυρίζεσθαι, ὡς καὶ ἐνίας τῶν γραφῶν περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ τολμᾶν ψευδεῖς λέγειν","issue":"The attachment of ἔχοντα is uncertain. The main text takes it as referring back to Peter in συννοῶ σε, so that Peter has the longing to insist and consequently dares to call passages false. It could formally modify τὸν δημιουργόν, yielding a sense such as ‘to show the Creator ... as having such a longing to insist,’ although that makes the following shift to Peter as the understood subject of τολμᾶν less direct. A looser construal making the Creator’s longing the content of Peter’s insistence would require διισχυρίζεσθαι to function separately rather than directly completing πόθον. No change to the supplied Greek is proposed.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"19.2","text":"“Do you say that there is a ruler of wickedness, or not? For if you say there is not, I can prove from many things, including statements of your teacher, that there is. But if you reasonably acknowledge that the evil one exists, I will carry the argument forward in due sequence.” Peter replied, “It is impossible for me to deny the voice of my teacher. I therefore acknowledge that the evil one exists, because the teacher who spoke truth in everything often said that he exists. For example, he acknowledges that the one who conversed with him for forty days had tested him. Somewhere else, too, I know that he said, ‘If Satan drives Satan out, he has become divided against himself. How, then, can his kingdom stand?’ He also made it clear that he had seen the evil one fall like lightning from heaven. Elsewhere he said, ‘The one who sowed the evil seed is the devil.’ And again, ‘Do not give the evil one an opportunity.’ In giving counsel he also said, ‘Let your yes be yes and your no, no; anything beyond these comes from the evil one.’ And in the prayer he handed down we have the words, ‘Rescue us from the evil one.’ Somewhere else, too, he promised to say to those who act impiously, ‘Go away into the outer darkness, which the Father prepared for the devil and his angels.’ So that I do not prolong the argument excessively, I know that my teacher often said that the evil one exists. Therefore I too agree that he exists. Now, if you have something to say as the next step, as you promised, say it.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"κακίας ἡγεμόνα","chosen":"a ruler of wickedness","rationale":"ἡγεμών denotes a leader or ruler; the phrase presents a personal power presiding over wickedness."},{"source_quote":"ἐκ πολλῶν καὶ τῶν τοῦ διδασκάλου σου","chosen":"from many things, including statements of your teacher","rationale":"The nouns governed by τῶν are implicit; ‘statements’ supplies the contextual sense without treating the teacher himself as evidence."},{"source_quote":"ἐπομένως ποιήσω τὸν λόγον","chosen":"I will carry the argument forward in due sequence","rationale":"ἐπομένως indicates a logically consequent or orderly next stage."},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας διαλεχθέντα πεπειρακέναι αὐτόν","chosen":"the one who conversed with him for forty days had tested him","rationale":"The accusative participle supplies the unexpressed subject of πεπειρακέναι, while αὐτόν is its object. Context favors the evil one as the tester and the teacher as the one tested, although neither referent is named within the clause."},{"source_quote":"μὴ δότε πρόφασιν τῷ πονηρῷ","chosen":"Do not give the evil one an opportunity","rationale":"πρόφασις can mean a pretext, occasion, or opportunity; ‘opportunity’ suits something granted to the evil one."},{"source_quote":"εἰπεῖν ὑπέσχετο","chosen":"he promised to say","rationale":"ὑπέσχετο ordinarily means ‘promised.’ The rendering is not harmonized to a familiar Gospel saying or softened to ‘threatened.’"},{"source_quote":"λοιπὸν εἴ τι ἔχεις ἐπομένως λέγειν","chosen":"Now, if you have something to say as the next step","rationale":"λοιπόν and ἐπομένως together mark the next consequence in Simon’s proposed argument."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"19.3","text":"Simon said, “Since, then, you have reasonably acknowledged that the evil one exists, tell us from the writings how he came to be—if indeed he came to be—and by whom and why.” Peter replied, “Pardon me, Simon, for not daring to say what has not been written. If you say that it has been written, show it. But if, since it has not been written, you too are unable to show it, why do we put ourselves in danger by making declarations about things not recorded? Or have we not believed that we will be judged, not only for what we do but also for what we say in belief, and is that why we speak more boldly about God?” Simon, understanding that this had been aimed at his recklessness, said, “Leave me to take the risk, but do not use what you call blasphemy as a pretext for retreat. For I perceive that you want to draw back so that you may escape being refuted before the crowds: at one time on the ground that you fear hearing blasphemies, and at another on the ground that, since it has not been written how, by whom, and why the evil one came to be, one must not dare to say more than Scripture. Therefore, as a reverent man, you confirm this alone: that he exists. But in devising these tactics you deceive yourself, not knowing that if it is blasphemy to investigate the evil one precisely, the responsibility lies with me, the accuser, not with you, the one defending God. And if the matter under investigation is unwritten and for that reason you do not wish to investigate it, there are certain adequate paths capable of demonstrating the matters under investigation no less than writings can. For example, is it not necessary that the evil one—whom you too say exists—be either originated or unoriginated?”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εὐγνωμονήσας","chosen":"reasonably","rationale":"The participle commends Peter as having acted with good sense or fairness in making the admission."},{"source_quote":"τὸ πῶς γέγονεν (εἴπερ γέγο[νε])","chosen":"how he came to be—if indeed he came to be","rationale":"The parenthetical qualification leaves open the possibility that the evil one did not originate."},{"source_quote":"περὶ ὧν πιστεύοντες λαλοῦμεν","chosen":"for what we say in belief","rationale":"πιστεύοντες may mean ‘while believing’ or ‘as matters of belief’; the chosen wording preserves the connection between belief and speech."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὴν ἀπόνοιαν αὐτοῦ","chosen":"aimed at his recklessness","rationale":"ἀπόνοια can denote folly, desperation, or reckless audacity. Simon understands Peter’s warning as directed at his own conduct."},{"source_quote":"τὸν ἐπὶ τῶν ὄχλων ἔλεγχον","chosen":"being refuted before the crowds","rationale":"ἔλεγχος can denote refutation, exposure, or censure; the public debate favors ‘refuted.’"},{"source_quote":"περὶ πονηροῦ ἀκριβοῦν","chosen":"to investigate the evil one precisely","rationale":"ἀκριβόω here means to ascertain exact details. ‘Give a precise account of the evil one’ is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ἡ αἰτία περὶ ἐμὲ τὸν κατήγορον τυγχάνει, οὐ περὶ σὲ τὸν συνηγοροῦντα τῷ θεῷ","chosen":"the responsibility lies with me, the accuser, not with you, the one defending God","rationale":"The legal contrast between an accuser and an advocate is preserved."},{"source_quote":"ἢ γενητὸν εἶναι ἢ ἀγένητον","chosen":"be either originated or unoriginated","rationale":"The pair concerns whether the evil one came into being. ‘Created or uncreated’ is possible but could narrow γενητός prematurely to deliberate creation."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Ἐπεὶ οὖν εὐγνωμονήσας ὡμολόγησ[ας] εἶναι τὸν πονηρόν, ἀπὸ γραφῶν ἡ[μῖν] λέγε τὸ πῶς γέγονεν (εἴπερ γέγο[νε]) καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος καὶ διὰ τί. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σ[ύγ]γνωθί μοι, Σίμων, μὴ τολμῶντι εἰπεῖν [ἃ] μὴ γέγραπται.","issue":"The selected, image-checked text contains square-bracketed sequences within several words and around ἃ. The translation follows the complete forms explicitly supplied by the selected text and adds no further restoration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὁτὲ μὲν ὡς δεδιὼς βλασ[φημί]ας ἀκοῦσαι, ὁτὲ δὲ (ἐπεὶ μὴ γέ[γρα]πται πῶς καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος καὶ διὰ τί [γέ]γονεν ὁ πονηρός)","issue":"The selected text again marks parts of words with square brackets. The translation follows the supplied completed forms βλασφημίας, γέγραπται, and γέγονεν without inventing additional wording.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὅτι μὴ, χρὴ πλεῖον τῆς γραφῆς τολμᾶν λέγειν","issue":"The printed comma after μὴ disrupts the contextually expected construction. The translation provisionally attaches μὴ to χρὴ, yielding ‘one must not dare,’ while preserving every supplied word.","proposed_reading":"ὅτι μὴ χρὴ πλεῖον τῆς γραφῆς τολμᾶν λέγειν","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"19.4","text":"Peter said, “It is necessary.” Simon replied, “Therefore, if he is originated, he came into being through God himself, who made everything: either begotten like a living creature, or projected as substance and coming about outside through mixture. For if the matter from which he came to be was outside him, whether animate or inanimate, he came to be either through God himself or from himself, or even arose from things that do not exist; he belongs to the class of things that are relative to something, or he always existed. Since, then, all the paths toward discovering him have, as I think, been distinguished here, it is necessary that he be discoverable by traveling one of them. One seeking an origin must therefore travel each path and, upon finding the responsible party, understand that he is subject to blame. Is that not so? What do you think?”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὡς ζῷον γεννηθεὶς","chosen":"begotten like a living creature","rationale":"The comparison presents ordinary animal generation as one possible mode of origin."},{"source_quote":"οὐσιωδῶς προβληθεὶς","chosen":"projected as substance","rationale":"The philosophical language describes a projection or emanation in respect of substance; ‘emanated substantially’ is a viable alternative."},{"source_quote":"ἔξω τῇ κράσει συμβεβηκώς","chosen":"coming about outside through mixture","rationale":"κρᾶσις denotes mixing or blending, while συμβαίνω can describe coming together or coming about. The precise cosmological mechanism remains compressed in the Greek."},{"source_quote":"ἡ ὕλη ἔμψυχος [οὖσα] ἢ ἄψυχος","chosen":"the matter ... whether animate or inanimate","rationale":"ἔμψυχος and ἄψυχος distinguish matter possessing life or soul from lifeless matter."},{"source_quote":"τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν","chosen":"he belongs to the class of things that are relative to something","rationale":"The phrase uses the philosophical category of relatives, things whose identity is stated in relation to something else. Under the alternative syntactic grouping, it describes the matter rather than the evil one."},{"source_quote":"π[ά]σης οὖν ὁδοῦ (ὡς οἶμαι) ἐνταῦθα διῃρημένης","chosen":"all the paths ... have, as I think, been distinguished here","rationale":"διαιρέω suggests an exhaustive division or differentiation of possible avenues of inquiry."},{"source_quote":"εὑρόντα τὸν αἴτιον ὑπὸ μέμψιν αὐτὸν εἶναι νοεῖν","chosen":"upon finding the responsible party, understand that he is subject to blame","rationale":"αὐτόν is taken as referring to the responsible cause or agent just found. It could grammatically be heard as referring back to the evil one, but the argument seeks whom to blame for his origin."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"[εἰ γὰρ] ἐκτὸς ἦν αὐτοῦ ἡ ὕλη ἔμψυχος [οὖσα] ἢ ἄψυχος, ὅθεν γέγονεν, ἢ δι’ αὐτοῦ [τοῦ] θεοῦ ἢ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων [συμ]βέβηκεν","issue":"The selected text explicitly marks εἰ γάρ, οὖσα, τοῦ, and part of συμβέβηκεν with square brackets. The translation follows these supplied readings without adding an independent restoration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἢ δι’ αὐτοῦ [τοῦ] θεοῦ ἢ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων [συμ]βέβηκεν, τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν ἢ αἰεὶ ἦν","issue":"The sequence is syntactically compressed. The main text carries the evil one forward as the implied subject of γέγονεν, συμβέβηκεν, ἐστίν, and ἦν because ὅθεν γέγονεν resumes the surrounding inquiry into how the evil one originated. Alternatively, ἡ ὕλη may remain the subject or controlling topic: the clauses would then concern the origin and status of the matter from which the evil one arose—whether that matter came through God, from itself, or from nonbeing, whether it belongs among relative or dependent things, or whether it always existed. No alteration of the supplied Greek is proposed.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἐκτὸς ἦν αὐτοῦ ἡ ὕλη","issue":"The referent of αὐτοῦ may be God, as the sequence most naturally suggests, or the evil one. The translation retains the pronoun ‘him’ rather than resolving it explicitly.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"π[ά]σης","issue":"The selected text prints the alpha of πάσης within square brackets. The translation follows the supplied completed word and supplies no additional restoration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"19.5","text":"Peter said, “It seems to me that if he is shown to have come into being through God, the one who made him should not yet be subject to blame, for perhaps his usefulness might prove more necessary than everything else. But if he should even be shown not to have come into being, but to have existed always, neither in this case is the Creator blameworthy, since he is superior to all things: even if he has been unable to put an end to a beginning that has no beginning because he lacks the nature required to do so; or if, though able, he does not abolish him, having judged it unjust to impose an end on one who received no beginning, and making allowance for one who is evil by nature because he cannot become anything else, even if he should have the desire to become something else. But if, while wanting to make him good, he were unable, even so he is good, because he wants to but cannot. And in the very respect in which he is powerless, he is the most powerful of all, because the possibility is left to no one else. But if there is someone else who is able and yet does not put matters right, then, in the respect in which he is able but does not put matters right, he stands acknowledged as evil, since he does not stop him, as though taking pleasure in the things done by him. But if that other cannot do so either, better is the one who, besides being unable, ‘does not hesitate’ to benefit us as far as possible.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"μήπως τὸ χρήσιμον αὐτοῦ πάντων ἀναγκαιότερον εὑρεθείη","chosen":"for perhaps his usefulness might prove more necessary than everything else","rationale":"μήπως introduces a cautious possibility here. It can also have the preventive force ‘lest his usefulness prove,’ but Peter’s argument depends on withholding blame because such usefulness may be discovered."},{"source_quote":"ὡς αἰεὶ ὢν","chosen":"to have existed always","rationale":"The phrase explains what it would mean for the evil one not to have come into being."},{"source_quote":"ἀνάρχῳ ἀρχῇ","chosen":"a beginning that has no beginning","rationale":"The deliberately paradoxical repetition of ἀρχή is preserved. ‘Beginningless principle’ is a more technical alternative."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὸ μὴ φύσιν ἔχειν","chosen":"because he lacks the nature required to do so","rationale":"The implicit subject is taken as the Creator, explaining his inability to end the beginningless being. It is also possible to take the subject as the beginningless being or principle: ‘because it has no such nature.’"},{"source_quote":"κακῷ πεφυκότι συγγνῶναι","chosen":"making allowance for one who is evil by nature","rationale":"πεφυκότι presents evil as the being’s natural condition, while συγγνῶναι denotes pardon or allowance. The infinitive is construed with the decision not to destroy him; alternatively, it may remain under ἄδικον κρίνας, producing ‘judging it unjust ... to pardon one who is evil by nature.’"},{"source_quote":"καὶ εἰ τοῦ γενέσθαι τὸ ἐπιθυμεῖν ἔχοι","chosen":"even if he should have the desire to become something else","rationale":"The complement ‘something else’ is carried forward from the immediately preceding clause; the Greek literally speaks of possessing the desire to become."},{"source_quote":"ἀγαθὸν ποιῆσαι θέλων","chosen":"while wanting to make him good","rationale":"ἀγαθόν is taken predicatively of the evil one. An alternative is ‘wanting to do something good,’ but the preceding question of whether the evil one can become otherwise favors the chosen rendering."},{"source_quote":"ἐν ᾧ ἀδυνατεῖ πάντων ἐστὶ δυνατώτατος","chosen":"in the very respect in which he is powerless, he is the most powerful of all","rationale":"The paradoxical juxtaposition of inability and supreme power is preserved rather than explained away."},{"source_quote":"μὴ κατορθῶν","chosen":"does not put matters right","rationale":"κατορθόω can mean to succeed, act rightly, or set something right. The argument concerns an able agent who fails to correct the evil situation."},{"source_quote":"κρείττων ὁ πρὸς τῷ ἀδυνατεῖν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμᾶς εὐεργετεῖν ‚οὐκ ὀκνῶν.‘","chosen":"better is the one who, besides being unable, ‘does not hesitate’ to benefit us as far as possible","rationale":"πρὸς τῷ with the infinitive means ‘in addition to,’ and κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν limits the beneficence to what is possible. The selected text’s quotation marks around οὐκ ὀκνῶν are represented by inner quotation marks."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, ἐὰν· ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ φανῇ γεγονὼς","issue":"The printed punctuation after ἐὰν interrupts the conditional phrase. The translation provisionally reads the condition continuously with ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ while altering no Greek wording.","proposed_reading":"Ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, ἐὰν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ φανῇ γεγονὼς","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"εἰ καὶ ἀνάρχῳ ἀρχῇ τέλος [ἐπιθ]εῖναι διὰ τὸ μὴ φύσιν ἔχειν οὐ δεδύ[νητ]αι, ἢ δυνατὸς ὢν οὐκ ἀναιρεῖ αὐ[τόν], ἄδικον κρίνας ἀρχὴν μὴ εἰλη[φ]ότι τέλος ἐπιθεῖναι","issue":"The selected text marks portions of ἐπιθεῖναι, δεδύνηται, αὐτόν, and εἰληφότι with square brackets. The translation follows the completed forms explicitly supplied by the selected text and makes no additional restoration.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
